## Rhodymenia pseudopalmata (Lamouroux) P Silva

* * *

Rhodymenia pseudopalmata

Description: Thallus erect to 10 cm long, fronds rising from a discoid holdfast, stipe terete expanding into a flat-shaped blade with marginal proliferations dividing diochotomously 1 to 4 times, each branch to 10 mm wide.

Habitat: Common, epilithic and epiphytic generally sublittoral to 30 m.

Distribution: Widespread in the British Isles generally on western shores of Ireland, Wales, Scotland, Wales and England. Europe: Portugal, Spain and France. Further afield: Canary Islands, the Azores and South Africa.

Similar Species: Other species of Rhodymenia, Phyllophora; Schottera nicaeensis and Stenogramme interrupta.

More recently, molecular studies have discovered a number of cryptic species that have similar to almost identical anatomy, morphology, and reproduction.
In Rhodymenia, growth of the vegetative thallus is caused by the activity of a group of apical cells, which divide both longitudinally and transversely. The diversity in the number of uniaxial to multiaxial forms is not well understood (Kumar et al., 2014a). Species of Rhodymenia have a relatively loose cortex of irregular-sized cells as compared to a closely related genus (Guiry, 1977). The thallus of Rhodymenia dissecta is differentiated into a single layer epidermis and a 6–10 layered cortex. The outer cortex is compact, two to three layered and composed of small rounded, isodiametric cells that are 10–40 μm in diameter. Whereas the inner cortical region is loose, three to five layered and composed of large spherical and vacuolated cells that are 100–200 μm in diameter. The cells of the inner cortex are irregularly arranged with intercellular mucilage filling the intercellular spaces. Guiry (1977) considered the inner cortex as the medullary region in Rhodymenia pseudopalmata. The epidermis also has a mucilaginous layer, which prevents the thallus from desiccation. Rhodymenia has the most species (54) in the family, a worldwide distribution, and occurs in temperate to cool water to depths of 100 m. Thalli are erect or prostrate and usually have blades on stipes that arise from a discoid base or stolon. The blades have a medulla of large axially elongated cells and a cortex of small cuboidal cells. Rhodymenia delicatula P.J.L. Dangeard (1949) is known throughout the North Atlantic and the Mediterranean; it is a small species (22-mm tall) with delicate blades that are dichotomously divided and attached by a creeping stolon. In contrast, a deep-water species, Rhodymenia pseudopalmata (J.V. Lamouroux) P.C. Silva (1952) is known from the Caribbean and eastern and North and tropical Atlantic; it has large blades (to 30 cm) that may be dichotomously or palmately divided and a discoid base (Plate 4.3Z). Male thalli have irregular patches or sori of spermatangia, while female gametophytes have three-celled carpogonial branches; after fertilization, cystocarps form on blade margins and are up to 1 mm in diameter.

## STRUCTURE AND DEVELOPMENT OF THE THALLUS

### EXTERNAL MORPHOLOGY

Plants of *Rhodymenia pseudopalmata* var. *ellisiae* formed erect, flattened fronds from stolons which were usually terete and were found to ramify extensively in soft rock or sponges. Stolons were colourless or lightly coloured when completely embedded and were branched irregularly, often resulting in large clumps of erect blades (Fig. 35C). Erect fronds had a dark crimson or purplish-red colour and were often spirally twisted (Fig. 35A). Some slight changes in the appearance of the erect blades were observed to take place throughout the growing season. Epiphytic specimens were not observed.

In the intertidal plants tended to grow gregariously. In March at Seaford, Sussex (27 March 1974) stolons of this variety were found ramifying in soft rock and forming short, upright, slightly flattened fronds. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
